# Dedaptive Testing <img src="man/figures/logo.png" align="right" alt="" width="120" />

<div style="clear: both;"></div>

<!-- badges: start -->
<!-- badges: end -->


The R package `dedaptive` provides tools for **DEcision-oriented aDAPTIVE testing** based on  
probabilistic latent variable models. Currently, the package supports **Multidimensional Item Response Theory (MIRT)** and **Unrestricted Latent Class (ULC)** 
models. The underlying methodological framework is described in Wyss et al. (2026). 

To install the development version, you need the package `remotes`. The package `dedaptive`can be installed with `remotes::install_github("Statric/dedaptive")`

This workflow demonstrates:

1. Loading the data set (`screenMental`) integrated into the package  
2. Fitting a MIRT (`fitIrt`) and ULC (`fitLc`) 
3. Simulation-based predictions of joint item distributions (`predJointDistResp`)
4. Performing probabilistic predictions with fixed-item panels (`fixSelection`) and adaptive, decision-oriented and cost-sensitive testing (`dedaptive`)
5. Simulating new item responses given predictor values (`simResponsesLatentModel`)  

## 1. Load and prepare the example data

We load the `dedaptive` package and the included data set `screenMental`, which serves as an example dataset to demonstrate the package's main functionalities throughout this workflow

```{r}
library(dedaptive)
data(screenMental)
head(screenMental, 3)
```

The `screenMental` data set is fully simulated to resemble item responses from the Patient Health Questionnaire 9 (PHQ-9) and Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale 7 (GAD-7) observed in a real clinical sample. The data were generated using a MIRT model fitted to the original data set analyzed in Wyss et al. (2026). The data generation process is included in Section 5 (*Simulating a data set*) below. The data set includes sex, age and responses to 16 questionnaire items: nine from the PHQ-9 and seven from the GAD-7. 

In the following examples, we focus on the joint distribution of the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 sum scores and corresponding binary decisions, defined by PHQ-9 sum score $\geq 10$ and GAD-7 sum score $\geq 10$, indicating at least moderate to severe symptoms. We first define functions to calculate the sum scores and specify the classification thresholds:

```{r}
# Extract PHQ-9 and GAD-7 items
itemsPhq<- colnames(screenMental)[grepl("phq", colnames(screenMental))]
itemsGad<- colnames(screenMental)[grepl("gad", colnames(screenMental))]
itemsAll<- c(itemsPhq, itemsGad)

# Score functions
funSumScores <- list(
  function(x) sum(x[1:9]),     # PHQ-9 sum score
  function(x) sum(x[10:16])    # GAD-7 sum score
)

# Thresholds
thresModSev <- c(10, 10)

# Add scores and decisions to the data set
screenMental$phq_score<- apply(screenMental[, itemsAll], 1, funSumScores[[1]])
screenMental$gad_score<- apply(screenMental[, itemsAll], 1, funSumScores[[2]])

screenMental$phq_dec<- ifelse(screenMental$phq_score>=thresModSev[1], 1, 0)
screenMental$gad_dec<- ifelse(screenMental$gad_score>=thresModSev[2], 1, 0)
```

We standardize age and prepare a training data set and a prediction data set containing a single individual:

```{r}
screenMental$ageStand<- (screenMental$age-mean(screenMental$age))/sd(screenMental$age)

idPred<- 400
screenMental[screenMental$id==idPred, ]

dataTrain <- screenMental[screenMental$id != idPred, ]
dataSub   <- screenMental[screenMental$id == idPred, ]
```

To illustrate the predictions, we consider a 37-year-old woman with a PHQ-9 sum score of 6 and a GAD-7 sum score of 3.

## 2. Fit latent variable models

Both supported models types (MIRT and ULC) can incorporate predictors of the latent variables or latent class membership and can subsequently be used for probabilistic predictions and adaptive item selections. 

The functions `fitIrt` and `fitLc` are wrappers around `mirt::mirt` and `poLCA::poLCA`, respectively, but tailored to the requirements of `dedaptive`. Therefore, models intended for use with `dedaptive` should be fitted using these functions rather than calling the underlying functions directly. 

### 2.1 Multidimensional Item Response Theory (MIRT) models
The function `fitIrt` fits multidimensional graded response models. The argument `model` specifies the latent structure, including the number of latent variables, item-factor relationships, and correlations between latent variables. 

In the following example, we fit a **two-factor model** in which all items load on both latent variables and the latent variables are assumed to be uncorrelated. Such a model can be specified by setting the argument `model` to 2 (number of latent variables).  The means of the latent variables are assumed to depend on age and sex through a latent regression, specified by the argument `formula`. 

```{r}
# Latent regression formula (right-hand side only)
whichFormula <- "ageStand + sex"

# Fit the two-factor IRT model
modelTrainIrt <- fitIrt(
  model   = 2,
  items   = itemsAll,
  formula = whichFormula,
  data    = dataTrain
)
```

The MIRT model itself is stored in `modelTrainIrt$fit`. For further details, see `?fitIrt` and `?mirt::mirt`. 

To select the number of latent factors based on information criteria such as **Akaike Information Criterion  (AIC)** or **Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC)**, the package provides the function `fitIrtSearchLatent`.

### 2.2 Unrestricted Latent Class (ULC) models

As an alternative to MIRT, the function `fitLc` fits unrestricted latent class models for categorical item responses. These models assume that individuals belong to one of a finite number of latent classes, with class-specific item response probabilities.

In the following example, we fit a **two-class latent class model**, including age and sex as predictors of latent class membership. The number of latent classes is specified by `nClasses`, while `formula` specifies the latent class regression. The argument `nrep` specifies the number of times the model is fitted using different random starting values, retaining the solution with the highest log-likelihood. This reduces the risk of convergence to a local rather than the global maximum of the likelihood function.

```{r}
# Fit a two-class latent class model
modelTrainLc <- fitLc(
  nClasses = 2,
  items    = itemsAll,
  formula  = whichFormula,
  data     = dataTrain,
  nrep     = 100,
  verbose=FALSE
)
```

The fitted ULC model is stored in `modelTrainLc$fit`. For further details, see `?fitLc` and `?poLCA::poLCA`. 

Similarly, the function `fitLcSearchLatent` allows selecting the number of latent classes based on AIC or BIC.


## 3. Predict joint item response distributions

The function `predJointDistResp` performs probabilistic predictions of joint item response distributions based on a MIRT or ULC model fitted with `fitIrt` or `fitLc`, respectively. The function can incorporate predictors via a latent regression and optionally condition on already observed responses for a subset of items.

By default, the joint distribution is approximated using a two-step Monte Carlo procedure: First, `nSimLatent` values of the latent variables (MIRT) or latent classes (ULC) are sampled from their predicted distribution. For each draw, `nSimItem` item response patterns are simulated, resulting in `nSimLatent * nSimItem` simulated response patterns in total. The joint distribution is then approximated by the relative frequencies of the simulated response patterns. Further details on this approximation strategy can be found in Wyss et al. (2026). For MIRT models, the joint item response distribution is always approximated through simulation, as no analytical solution is available. For ULC models, the argument `fullJoint = TRUE` additionally allows exact computation of the joint distribution. However, because the number of possible response patterns increases exponentially with the number of items, simulation-based approximation is generally more computationally efficient for larger questionnaires.

### 3.1 Prior predictions

We first illustrate predictions for the held-out individual in `dataSub`, assuming that no item responses are known. Thus, predictions are based only on age and sex through the latent regression.

```{r}
predJointPrior <- predJointDistResp(
  model     = modelTrainIrt,
  dataSub   = dataSub,
  nSimLatent = 1000,
  nSimItem  = 10,
  seed      = 123
)
head(predJointPrior$jointDist, 3)
```
The resulting object `predJointPrior` contains

- a table with all `nSimLatent * nSimItem` simulated response patterns (`predJointPrior$sim`), and

- a table with the unique response patterns and their relative frequencies of unique response patterns (`predJointPrior$jointDist`).

The same function and arguments can be used for ULC models by replacing `modelTrainIrt` with `modelTrainLc`.

### 3.2 Conditional predictions

The function can also predict joint item response distributions conditional on already observed responses for a subset of items. To illustrate this, we assume that the first PHQ-9 and GAD-7 items have been answered with `phq1 = 1` and `gad1 = 1`.

```{r}
# Define the given responses
whichResp<- c(phq1=1, gad1=1)

# Conditional predictions
predJointCond <- predJointDistResp(
  model      = modelTrainIrt,
  dataSub    = dataSub,
  nSimLatent = 1000,
  nSimItem   = 10,
  givenVal   = whichResp,
  seed       = 123
)
```

As with prior predictions, the resulting objects contain the simulated response patterns (`sim`) and their relative frequencies (`jointDist`). In addition, conditional predictions return the posterior joint distribution of the latent variables in `postDistLatent`, accounting for the observed item responses and predictors (if specified). For ULC models, `postDistLatent` contains the posterior latent class membership probabilities.

## 4. Fixed and dedaptive item selections

The function `fixSelection` performs probabilistic predictions based on the observed responses to a **fixed subset of items**. In contrast, `dedaptive` **adaptively selects** items to minimize expected costs of misclassification and measurement. After each selected item, the observed response is incorporated into the probabilistic predictions. The procedure stops when selecting another item is no longer expected to reduce total costs. The function also returns predictions based on the final, individualized set of selected items

Both functions provide probabilistic predictions for

1. the latent variables (`distLatent`),

2. the score functions (e.g., PHQ-9 and GAD-7 sum scores in this example) and the corresponding binary decisions (e.g., PHQ-9 / GAD-7 sum score $\geq 10$; `distFun`), and  

3. the response patterns of the remaining items (`distItems`).  

In addition, the component `pred` summarizes predicted scores, classification probabilities, true scores and decisions, and the number of selected items.

Both functions require all item responses to be available in `dataSub`, allowing the true scores and decisions to be calculated for comparison with the predictions. However, only the responses to the selected items are used for prediction.

The following examples use the MIRT model fitted in Section 2. The same functions and arguments can also be used with the ULC model by replacing `modelTrainIrt` with `modelTrainLc`.

### 4.1 Fixed-item selections

We first illustrate `fixSelection`, using only the item responses of the short forms PHQ-2 and GAD-2 to perform probabilistic predictions:


```{r}
# Define the fixed subset of items
itemsShortVersion <- c("phq1", "phq2", "gad1", "gad2")

# Show the observed responses
dataSub[, itemsShortVersion, drop = FALSE]

# Perform probabilistic predictions
predShortVersion <- fixSelection(
  model      = modelTrainIrt,
  dataSub    = dataSub,
  thres      = thresModSev,
  funOfItems = funSumScores,
  givenVar   = itemsShortVersion,
  nSimLatent = 1000,
  nSimItem   = 10,
  seed       = 13
)

# Show summary predictions
predShortVersion$pred

```

The resulting object `predShortVersion$pred` contains predicted and true sum scores, probabilities of exceeding the thresholds, and true binary decisions. The component `distFun` contains the predicted joint distribution of the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 sum scores and their corresponding decisions.

### 4.2 Dedaptive item selection

We now use `dedaptive` to select items sequentially, optimizing the two binary decisions defined by the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 thresholds.

For dedaptive testing, we specify the costs of false-positive (FP) and false-negative (FN) classifications for each decision, as well as a measurement cost per selected item (via the argument `costs`). Here, we assign equal costs of 0.5 to false-positive and false-negative classifications for each decision and a measurement cost of 0.05 per item.

```{r}
# Define classification and measurement costs
prescribedCosts <- list(
  c(0.5, 0.5),  # False-positive costs for PHQ-9 and GAD-7
  c(0.5, 0.5),  # False-negative costs for PHQ-9 and GAD-7
  0.05          # Measurement cost per item
)

# Perform dedaptive item selection
predDedaptive <- dedaptive(
  model      = modelTrainIrt,
  dataSub    = dataSub,
  thres      = thresModSev,
  funOfItems = funSumScores,
  costs      = prescribedCosts,
  nSimLatent = 1000,
  nSimItem   = 10,
  seed       = 13
)

# Show summary predictions
predDedaptive$pred

# Show the selected items and their observed responses
dataSub[, predDedaptive$chosen, drop = FALSE]
```

At each step, dedaptive evaluates the expected reduction in misclassification costs from administering each remaining item. The item with the lowest expected total cost, including its measurement cost, is selected. Selection stops when no additional item is expected to reduce total costs.

The output `predDedaptive$chosen` contains the selected items in the order in which they were administered. The component `predDedaptive$pred` summarizes the final probabilistic predictions and the number of selected items.

### 4.3 Visualizing predictions

For two score functions and corresponding binary decisions, `plotScoresItemSelection` visualizes their predicted joint distribution.

```{r, fig.width=7,fig.height=7, fig.cap="Fig. 2 posterior distribution of the scores with fixed item selection"}
# Fixed-item selection
plotScoresItemSelection(
  predShortVersion,
  main = "Fixed-item selection",
  xlab = "PHQ-9 sum score",
  ylab = "GAD-7 sum score"
)
```

```{r, fig.width=7,fig.height=7, fig.cap="Fig. 3 posterior distribution of the scores with dedaptive item selection"}
# Dedaptive item selection
plotScoresItemSelection(
  predDedaptive,
  main = "Dedaptive item selection",
  xlab = "PHQ-9 sum score",
  ylab = "GAD-7 sum score"
)
```

The central panels show the predicted joint distributions of the PHQ-9 (x-axis) and GAD-7 (y-axis) sum scores. Each point represents a possible score combination, with its size and color indicating the predicted probability. Dashed lines mark the classification thresholds of 10, while the marginal distributions of each score are shown along the axes.

These plots illustrate how the predicted score distributions and classification probabilities differ between a predefined short-item panel and an individualized, decision-oriented adaptive selection.


## 5. Simulating a data set

The function `simResponsesLatentModel` simulates item responses based on a fitted MIRT or LC model, optionally conditional on predictor variables through a latent regression. This function was also used to generate the simulated data set `screenMental` included in the package, using models fitted to the original clinical data analyzed in Wyss et al. (2026).

In the following, we illustrate how to generate a new synthetic data set based on `screenMental`. We first fit a MIRT model to the entire data set using the same model specification as in Section 2.

```{r}
# Fit the MIRT model to the full data set
modelAllData <- fitIrt(
  model   = 2,
  items   = itemsAll,
  formula = whichFormula,
  data    = screenMental
)
```

Given this model, we can simulate item responses for specified predictor values. The function generates one response pattern for each row of `dataPred`.


```{r}
# Example: Woman and man with different standardized ages
simResponsesLatentModel(
  model    = modelAllData,
  dataPred = data.frame(
    ageStand = c(-1, 1),
    sex      = c(1, 0)
  ),
  seed = 13
)
```

The same function can be used with an LC model fitted using fitLc, without changing the other arguments.

To generate an entire synthetic data set, we first simulate new values for sex and age. We estimate the marginal distribution of sex and the sex-specific age distributions from `screenMental`, using kernel density estimation for age. We then sample sex from its marginal distribution and age conditional on sex. The following helper function, simulateSexAge, implements this procedure (it is not part of the dedaptive package).


```{r}
simulateSexAge <- function(data, nSim,
                           sexVar = "sex",
                           ageVar = "age", ...) {
  # 1) Prepare 
  sex <- data[[sexVar]]
  age <- data[[ageVar]]
  
  # Remove missing
  okCases <- stats::complete.cases(sex, age)
  sex <- sex[okCases]
  age <- age[okCases]
  
  # 2) Estimate distribution P(sex), f(age | sex)
  
  # Marginal distribution of sex
  sexTab  <- table(sex)
  sexProb <- prop.table(sexTab)
  sexVals <- sort(unique(sex))
  
  # Kernel densities for age within each sex
  densityList <- lapply(sexVals, function(s) {
    stats::density(age[sex == s], ...)
  })
  #names(densityList) <- sexVals
  
  # helper: sample from a 1D kernel density estimate
  sampleFromDensity <- function(d, n) {
    cdf <- cumsum(d$y)
    cdf <- cdf / max(cdf)
    u <- stats::runif(n)
    idx <- findInterval(u, vec = c(0, cdf), rightmost.closed = TRUE)
    d$x[pmax(1, idx)]
  }
  
  # 3) Simulate from estimated joint distribution
  # Simulate sex from its marginal
  simSexChar <- sample(sexVals, size = nSim, replace = TRUE, prob = sexProb)
  
  # Simulate age conditional on sex
  simAge <- numeric(nSim)
  for (s in 1:length(sexVals)) {
    idx <- which(simSexChar == sexVals[s])
    if (length(idx) > 0) {
      simAge[idx] <- sampleFromDensity(densityList[[s]], length(idx))
    }
  }
  
  simData <- data.frame(
    sex = simSexChar,
    age = simAge
  )
  
  # Return simulations plus estimated components
  list(
    sim = simData,
    sexProb = sexProb,
    ageDensities = densityList
  )
}
```

We first generate a data set with simulated sex and age values and visualize the underlying distribution estimates:

```{r, fig.width=5, fig.height=3, fig.cap="Fig. 4 Estimated age distributions by sex"}
# Apply the function simulateSexAge
# (includes distribution estimates besides the simulated data)
listSim<- simulateSexAge(screenMental, nrow(screenMental), "sex", "age")

# Extract densities and sex distribution
densList <- listSim$ageDensities
probFemale<- as.numeric(listSim$sexProb[2])

# Extract simulated data
dataSim<- listSim$sim

# Visualize the distribution estimates
plot(densList[[2]],
     xlab = "Age",
     ylab = "Density", 
     main="",
     lwd  = 2, 
     lty=1, cex.axis=0.6)

lines(densList[[1]], lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright",
       legend = c(paste0("sex = female (",round(probFemale*100), "%)"), 
                  paste0("sex = male (",round((1-probFemale)*100), "%)")), 
       lty    = c(1, 2),
       lwd    = 2,
       bty    = "n", cex=0.8)

# Round the age to a resolution of one year
dataSim$age<- round(dataSim$age)

# Assign age of 18 for persons younger than 18
dataSim$age[dataSim$age < 18]<- 18

# Show first rows
head(dataSim, 3)
```
Of note, we also rounded age to the nearest year (1-year resolution) and set all ages below 18 to 18. Finally, we standardize age using the mean and standard deviation of the original `screenMental` data set and simulate item responses conditional on sex and age using the function `simResponsesLatentModel`. 

```{r}
# Standardize the age (mean and SD from screenMental)
dataSim$ageStand<- (dataSim$age-mean(screenMental$age))/sd(screenMental$age)

# Simulate item responses given sex and age
dataSim <- simResponsesLatentModel(
  model    = modelAllData,
  dataPred = dataSim,
  seed     = 13
)

# Remove standardized age 
dataSim$ageStand<- NULL

head(dataSim,3)
```

The resulting `dataSim` is a fully simulated dataset containing sex, age, and PHQ-9/GAD-7 item responses. It approximately preserves the distributions and dependencies represented by the fitted models without directly reusing individual-level observations from `screenMental`.
